sections.heading: Define the possible outcomes first
sections.body:
A probability from 0 to 1 describes likelihood under a specified model. In a finite elementary model, zero means impossible and one means certain. For equally likely outcomes, divide favourable outcomes by total outcomes.

A fair six-sided die has six equally likely faces. “Greater than four” contains 5 and 6, so its probability is 2/6 = 1/3. Counting faces is insufficient for a biased die: equal likelihood is an assumption doing real work.

An event's complement contains all outcomes outside it, with probability one minus the event probability. The chance of not rolling a six is therefore 5/6.

Probability does not schedule compensation. After several sixes, an independent fair die does not owe you another result. Long-run proportions tend to stabilise over many trials, but short runs can look uneven without contradicting the model. An unusual real sequence can motivate checking whether fairness and independence are reasonable assumptions.
sections.visual: Picture six equal-size tiles labelled with die faces. Shade 5 and 6, then shade only the even numbers — the overlap is the event 'even and greater than 4'.

questions.q: After five sixes, what is the next-roll chance of six for an independent fair die?
questions.hint: The stated model gives the die no memory.
questions.answer: It remains 1/6. Earlier outcomes do not change the next-roll probability under the fair, independent model.

sections.heading: “And” and “or” use different rules
sections.body:
For two events A and B, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Here “or” includes both happening. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting those outcomes twice.

On a fair die, A = “even” contains 2, 4 and 6, while B = “greater than three” contains 4, 5 and 6. Their union contains 2, 4, 5 and 6. Its probability is 3/6 + 3/6 − 2/6 = 4/6.

For “and,” P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B given A). Independence lets the second factor become P(B). Two independent fair coin tosses are both heads with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. They differ from independent events: on one die roll, learning that “one” occurred makes “two” impossible. For positive-probability events, that information changes the probability rather than leaving it alone.
sections.visual: Picture two overlapping circles. Count their shared lens once for 'or.' Beside them, a tree of sequential choices multiplies probabilities along each path.

questions.q: Why are “roll a one” and “roll a two” not independent on the same roll?
questions.hint: What does knowing the first do to the second?
questions.answer: Knowing the roll is one changes the probability of two from 1/6 to zero. The events are mutually exclusive.

sections.heading: Choose the right denominator
sections.body:
Imagine 1,000 manufactured parts: 10 defective and 990 sound. A scanner flags 9 defective parts and falsely flags 99 sound parts. These are illustrative round numbers, not measured performance for a real product.

There are 108 flags in total. Of those, only 9 are true defects, so the defective fraction among flags is 9/108, about 8.3%. The scanner detects 90% of defective parts, yet a randomly selected flagged part is much less than 90% likely to be defective in this batch.

The conditional questions use different denominators. P(flagged given defective) selects the defective group; P(defective given flagged) selects the flagged group. The low base rate of defects means many sound parts can enter the flagged group despite a moderate false-positive rate.

Before interpreting a positive signal, identify the starting rate, detection rate and false-positive rate. Counting the relevant group explicitly can make a reversed conditional much easier to reason about.
sections.visual: Picture a tray of 1,000 parts with only 10 defects. Move 9 defective and 99 sound parts into a 'test positive' bin — most positives are false when the condition is rare.

questions.q: Which denominator answers “what fraction of flagged parts are defective”?
questions.answer: Use all 108 flagged parts. Nine are defective, so the fraction is 9/108, approximately 8.3%.

questions.q: What is the chance of a fair die showing more than four?
questions.explain: Faces 5 and 6 are favourable: two out of six, or 1/3.

questions.q: An event has probability 0.28. What is its complement probability?
What is the chance of “even or greater than three” on a fair die?
questions.explain: The union is 2, 4, 5 and 6: four of six. Adding without subtracting the overlap double-counts 4 and 6.

questions.q: Two independent fair tosses are both heads with what probability?
questions.explain: Multiply 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. This is both heads, not at least one head.

questions.q: How many parts are flagged in the example?
questions.explain: Add 9 true positives to 99 false positives to obtain 108 flags.

questions.q: Why does 90% detection not mean 90% of flags are true defects?
choices: The conditions select different groups, and the base rate matters
questions.explain: Detection divides by defective parts. Reliability of a flag divides by all flagged parts, including false positives.
